title: AI Overviews Are Rewiring Search: What Changed in 2026
content:
Screenshot of blog.google (source)

Here's my bottom line: AI Overviews didn't kill search traffic in 2026 - they repriced it. In my reading of the data, informational "how do I do X" content has lost a large share of its clicks when an AI Overview appears, and generic comparison content is also heavily affected (see Seer's 95.4% figure below). Content built on firsthand input, such as original testing and verified pricing, looks like the more defensible position. If you're still measuring your site's health by total organic sessions, you're tracking the wrong number and you're about to make some very bad decisions.

The less visible part is behavioral: Pew's browsing data shows people click traditional results less often when an AI summary appears, and online publishers have attributed declining web traffic to those summaries.

What's Actually Going On

Screenshot of pewresearch.org (source)

The scale is bigger than most people realize

This is no longer a niche feature. At Google I/O in May 2026, Sundar Pichai said AI Overviews had passed 2.5 billion monthly active users, and AI Mode - the conversational search experience - had surpassed 1 billion monthly active users in roughly a year . Google also said AI Mode queries have been more than doubling every quarter since launch (Google Search I/O 2026 post).

For context on how fast that moved: Pichai described AI Mode as passing 1 billion monthly active users in just a year. At this scale, treating it as a passing experiment is hard to justify (my opinion).

The click data is ugly, but it's ugly selectively

Pew's study is useful because it tracked real browsing rather than keyword-tool estimates. Analyzing 900 U.S. adults' browsing data, Pew found 58% of users ran at least one search that triggered an AI summary in March 2025; users clicked a traditional result link in 8% of visits to search pages with an AI summary versus 15% of visits without one; clicks on links inside the summaries happened in only 1% of visits; and users were more likely to abandon browsing after a page with a summary (26%) than without (16%).

Google disputed Pew's methodology, arguing the analysis period overlapped with unrelated algorithm testing.

Ahrefs, using a different method entirely, landed in the same direction. Their April 2025 comparison of forecasted vs. actual CTR suggested AI Overviews reduced position-1 click-through rate by about 34.5%; Ahrefs' February 2026 re-run, using December 2025 data, put the figure at about 58% (source) , and notably, 99.2% of keywords that trigger AI Overviews are informational in intent .

That last stat is the whole story, and almost nobody leads with it.

The rebound is real - and it's a redistribution, not a recovery

Seer Interactive's longitudinal study is the most useful 2026 dataset I've seen. It covers 53 brands, 5.47 million queries, and 2.43 billion impressions from January 2025 to February 2026.

CTR on AI Overview queries bottomed at 1.3% in December 2025 and climbed back to 2.4% by February 2026 - an 85% jump in two months.

But look at what happened on the other side of the ledger: CTR on searches without AI Overviews rose from 2.8% in early 2025 to 3.8% by February 2026. One plausible reading (mine, not a measured finding) is that AI Overviews absorb the quick answers, so the users who still click are the ones who want more.

Cited pages outperform uncited pages on the same results page, but both still trail no-AIO searches.

And Seer's query-type breakdown contains the one finding that should reset a lot of assumptions: at a 95.4% AIO trigger rate, nearly every "X vs Y" informational query in their study had an AI Overview - meaning comparison-page traffic is almost certainly AIO-affected.

My Take

Screenshot of seerinteractive.com (source)

The dominant narrative - "AI Overviews are destroying the open web" - is emotionally satisfying and strategically useless. A framing I find more useful is that Google automated the part of the web that was low-value: the 900-word article that exists solely to restate a fact you could have gotten in one sentence.

I don't think that's a tragedy. I think it was overdue. The "how to convert PDF to Word" genre was never content; it was a toll booth built on top of an answer. Google removed the toll booth. Of course traffic fell.

One point worth stating: the declines are not uniform. Pew found just 8% of one- or two-word searches produced an AI summary, rising to 53% for searches of 10 words or more - the long, conversational, explain-this-to-me query is AI Overview territory. The short, brand-specific, "I already know what I want" query largely isn't. Those are different businesses with different futures, and averaging them into one "organic traffic" line hides that completely.

Here's where I'll get specific, because the data pushes in an uncomfortable direction: the comparison-content safe harbor is closing. For most of 2025, the advice was "pivot to comparison and buying-intent content, AI Overviews don't touch it." Seer's 95.4% AIO rate on "X vs Y" queries says that window is basically shut for generic comparisons. What survives isn't the format, it's the input - original testing, real pricing you actually paid, screenshots, opinions a model can't synthesize from three other summaries. An AI Overview can compress consensus. It can't manufacture a firsthand judgment that doesn't exist on the web yet.

To the skeptical reader who says "this is just SEOs whining about a platform change": partly, yes. But the second-order effect is real. Pew's data showed Reddit, Wikipedia, and YouTube among the most-cited sources in AI summaries - when synthesis pays and origination doesn't, you get more synthesis and fewer people doing the original work that synthesis depends on. That's a slow problem, not a loud one, which is exactly why it's easy to ignore.

The Counterpoint

Screenshot of ahrefs.com (source)

The strongest argument against me is that clicks were always a bad proxy for value, and the CTR rebound proves the panic was overblown. Seer cautions that a CTR drop isn't automatically bad news: if clicks held steady while impressions rose, a site may simply have earned more citations. If AI Overviews strip out the low-intent drive-by visitors who were never going to convert, a site can lose 40% of its sessions and lose almost nothing that mattered. Fair. Some of the loudest traffic-collapse stories are businesses discovering their audience was never really theirs.

I still land where I started, for one reason: even cited pages get fewer clicks than pages on no-AIO searches . Being the source Google trusts most is still worse, click-wise, than the AI simply not showing up. That's not a quality filter. That's a structural discount on being on the web at all.

Bottom Line

If you run a content site, a SaaS blog, or a personal brand that depends on search:

  • Stop reporting total organic sessions. Split your reporting into AIO-present and AIO-absent queries. They're two different channels now with opposite trend lines.
  • Reconsider your explainer backlog. In my view, content whose only job is to state a fact is a depreciating asset in 2026. Redirect that effort into things requiring firsthand input - tests, teardowns, pricing you verified, opinions with a name attached.
  • Treat citation as a real KPI, but don't pretend it replaces traffic. Cited pages earn roughly 2.1% CTR versus about 0.9% for uncited pages on the same results page - worth chasing, not worth betting the business on.
  • Build one channel Google can't intermediate. Email, community, podcast, YouTube. Pick one and actually work it.

For searchers, open the underlying sources for prices, recent changes and judgment calls. Check dates and whether the source actually supports the answer. This is a practical verification recommendation, not a measured claim about AI Overview accuracy.

FAQ

Are AI Overviews reducing clicks for every kind of search? No. Ahrefs found 99.2% of AI Overview–triggering keywords are informational in intent , and Pew found only 8% of one- or two-word searches produced a summary versus 53% of searches with 10+ words . Per Pew, short searches are far less likely to trigger an AI summary than long conversational ones.

Is the CTR decline reversing? Partially - Seer measured a bottom of 1.3% in December 2025 rising to 2.4% by February 2026. But CTR on searches without AI Overviews rose to 3.8% over the same period , so the gap hasn't closed.

Does getting cited in an AI Overview make up for lost traffic? It helps and it isn't enough. Pew found clicks on links inside AI summaries occurred in just 1% of visits . Citation is better than invisibility; it is not a traffic strategy on its own.

Is AI Mode a bigger threat than AI Overviews? Not yet in raw reach - AI Overviews sit above 2.5 billion monthly users versus AI Mode's 1 billion - but AI Mode queries have been more than doubling every quarter , so the trajectory matters more than the current gap.

Correction note (October 2026): This post was revised to update the Ahrefs click-through figure (34.5% in April 2025; about 58% in its February 2026 re-run), remove unsupported absolutes, align the bottom-line claim about comparison content with Seer's data, and clarify that Pew's click rates refer to visits to search pages. Sources: Ahrefs, Pew Research Center, Seer Interactive, Google.
